<reason>CON built a tighter, more disciplined case: a clear necessity/proportionality standard, a real distinction between anonymous credential-verification and person-verification, a sharp gambling-vs-pornography distinction (transaction control vs. content circulation) that it defended cleanly under pressure, and an exclusion argument that pushed back on PRO's "mere friction" framing. Crucially, CON's rebuttal that digital content can be forwarded/linked without needing a "supplier" (unlike alcohol or cigarettes) directly undercut PRO's central alcohol/cigarette analogy, and PRO never squarely answered that disanalogy in later rounds, instead re-asserting the same analogy. PRO's closing pivot ("CON's alternative is also unproven, so weigh the stakes") was a good rhetorical move and did expose that CON's own alternative was unproven, but CON's answer — that the burden for compelling a mandate lies with the proponent, not with critics to prove an alternative — is a legitimate and standard response that PRO did not dismantle. PRO's opening was also clipped by the word limit, costing it a full framing of its case. Overall CON answered pressure more directly and left fewer of its own claims exposed, giving it the cleaner path to victory, though the debate was close and both sides argued competently.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal in [A2.2]/[A4.4] — pointing out that unlike physical goods (alcohol, cigarettes), pornographic content can be forwarded or linked without needing a supplier, so the alcohol/cigarette "leakage" analogy PRO relied on throughout does not transfer — was the most damaging unanswered point, since PRO never directly confronted this disanalogy in its subsequent rebuttal or closing.</best_rebuttal>
